paras: The lynching of Sam Adams was the hanging of a young Black man by residents of Pass Christian, Mississippi, on the night of November 5, 1903, after he was accused of assaulting Mrs. Peter Labouisse, a white woman, that afternoon. He was taken from officers who were moving him from the jail, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of "male citizens, both white and colored," organized to kill him. The case drew national notice because Mrs. Labouisse had been a New York society figure.

Pass Christian was described as a coast resort of New Orleans people whose small Black population consisted mainly of domestic servants. The Sun gave Adams's age as 18; the Hattiesburg Daily Progress called him a butcher.

According to the dispatches, Adams unhitched Mrs. Labouisse's horse while she gathered flowers with a maid, then told her it had strayed and drew her away to recover it. The Sun and the Evening World said he seized her by the throat and drew a knife, then fled when she screamed.

A posse, which the Evening World said included white and Black men, fired on Adams and caught him within about half an hour, and after she identified him he was jailed under armed guard. That night officers set out to move him to Mississippi City, but he was taken from them and hanged from a tree near town. The Evening World said he was given five minutes to pray and that "both whites and negroes" pulled the rope.

At an inquest on November 7 the coroner's jury found that Adams died at the hands of citizens "organized and determined" to kill him for "the crime that meets death" wherever committed. The Sun reported that a proposal to expel all Black residents was dropped after they expressed "horror of the crime and approval of the lynching." A later dispatch said Adams's father was ordered to leave the county and that the lynchers were "all well known, but no movement will be made against them"; no report of arrests appears in the coverage. The Evening World reported that Mrs. Labouisse had protested against the lynching.

The Associated Press story ran on November 6 in papers from Indiana to Montana, where the Butte Inter Mountain headed it "SUMMARY JUSTICE." The wire stated the assault as fact; the Indianapolis Journal's headline read "Criminally Assaulted a White Woman and Was Promptly Punished." The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, the only Mississippi paper with its own Pass Christian report, called the lynching "the inevitable result in such cases."

New York papers centered their stories on Mrs. Labouisse's marriages and family. A follow-up wire headed "War on Bad Blacks" called the lynching "the culmination of negro outlawry in that section," and the verdict ran as "Jury Justifies Lynching" in the New-York Tribune and as a "Strange Verdict" elsewhere.

On November 15 the Sun printed a dispatch headed "AN IDEAL LYNCHING, THEY SAY," describing a mass meeting at the Knights of Honor Hall that named a committee of seven whites and three Black men, the latter "at their own request," to carry out the hanging. It named Charles Cornell, the Black assistant principal of the public school, as a speaker for the lynching. The Newton Times, reprinted in the Okolona Messenger, praised the open hanging of "the ravisher" and had "no regrets" that there was no trial.

The St. Paul Appeal noted that the coroner's jury "justified the work of the mob," while calling Adams "the Afro-American who assaulted Mrs. Peter Labouisse," and the Chicago Broad Ax listed him in its year-end lynching chronology.

The Hattiesburg special said guards surrendered Adams to about a hundred men, the Evening World said a constable gave him up, and the Sun's first report said the officers were knocked down and "severely injured." The offense was reported as a completed criminal assault by the wire, as a knifepoint seizure by the Sun and Evening World, and as an "attempting assault" by the Pawtucket Gazette.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam Adams
bases: Adams, accused of assaulting a white woman, was taken from officers by a crowd or appointed committee and hanged from a tree without trial (A4, A8, A28).

Adams was hanged by about a hundred men (A4) or a ten-member committee named by a mass meeting (A28), with no trial, as punishment for an accused assault on a white woman; the coroner's jury itself described organized citizens 'determined to finish' him (A17).

The AP wire (A3), a Pass Christian special to a Mississippi paper (A4), separate New Orleans dispatches (A8, A9) and the coroner's verdict (A17, A18) agree that Adams was taken from officers and hanged on the night of Nov. 5.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Adams 'criminally assaulted' Mrs. Labouisse after luring her away by cutting her horses loose; he was captured and a mob took him from a guarded jail and hanged him, overpowering officers bound for Mississippi City.

accounts.label: Pass Christian special (Hattiesburg)
accounts.gist: Guards taking Adams away to save him were met by about a hundred men, surrendered him, and he was hanged minutes later by 'a very orderly and determined mob'.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatches (Sun, Evening World)
accounts.gist: Adams seized her throat and drew a knife, then fled when she screamed; a posse shot at and caught him; officers moving him were attacked (Sun) or a constable gave him up (Evening World); whites and Blacks pulled the rope.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Adams died at the hands of white and colored male citizens organized and determined to kill him for 'the crime that meets death'.

accounts.label: Later New Orleans dispatch ('Ideal lynching')
accounts.gist: A town mass meeting appointed a committee of seven whites and three Black men which ran Adams down and hanged him quietly; he made no denial; no action would be taken against the lynchers.

accounts.label: Black press
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Appeal reported that the coroner's jury justified the mob; the Broad Ax listed the case in its year-end lynching chronology.

framing.detail: AP wire states the assault as fact under heads such as 'SUMMARY JUSTICE' and 'Criminally Assaulted a White Woman and Was Promptly Punished'.
Hattiesburg special: 'Brute Assaults Lady and is Summarily Dealt With by Mob', the lynching 'the inevitable result in such cases'.
New York papers center Mrs. Labouisse's society background; the Evening World headlines that she 'VAINLY PROTESTED AGAINST THE LYNCHING'; the Evening Journal calls the verdict 'Strange'.
Follow-up wire 'War on Bad Blacks' calls the lynching 'the culmination of negro outlawry' and forecasts expulsions along the coast.
Sun's 'AN IDEAL LYNCHING, THEY SAY' reports Mississippi approval of the committee method, attributing the praise to others.
Newton Times (via Okolona Messenger) praises the open hanging of 'the ravisher' and has 'no regrets' there was no trial.
St. Paul Appeal notes the jury 'justified the work of the mob' while calling Adams 'the Afro-American who assaulted' Mrs. Labouisse, without comment; Broad Ax lists the case in a chronology.
